newsitem.title: UK: UK housing market ends 1996 on a high-survey.
newsitem.headline: UK housing market ends 1996 on a high-survey.

text.p: Britain's housing market is ending 1996 on a high in terms of the number of properties sold, The Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors said on Tuesday.
The average number of properties sold per chartered surveyor rose to its highest level this year over the three months to the end of November, the latest RICS survey showed.

Neither a late-October increase in official interest rates nor uncertainty about what Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke would unveil in his November 26 budget could dampen the market's optimism, the RICS said.
Prices were boosted modestly by a still-severe shortage of properties on the market. A net balance of 44 percent of chartered surveyors reported higher prices.
The picture should be little-changed next year as potential buyers receive windfalls from building society mergers and flotations and the effects of budget tax cuts filter through.
"The outlook for 1997 is that prices will continue to be bolstered by the strength of the economy and tax cuts," RICS housing market spokesman, Ian Perry said.
"However, they will be tempered by the interest rate rises we are likely to see next year and by an influx of properties coming onto the market."

He said prices would continue to rise fastest in the south, where the number of households blighted by negative equity -- where the property of a house is worth less than the mortgage taken out on it -- would fall by 100,000 to 150,000 by the autumn of 1997.
"The rapid elimination of negative equity means that more households will at last be free to move," Perry said.

The survey also forecast extravagant bonuses paid by banks and investment and securities houses in the City of London would fuel demand at the upper end of the market in the south-east early next year.
Over the last three months, the trend of four bedroom houses and country houses showing consistent price rises across the regions has continued, the survey said.
Regionally, chartered surveyors in East Anglia saw a marked rise in prices over the past three months while the south east remained strong.
